# Skylar Zinnecker CMJ Return-to-Competition Reports

A series of CMJ (countermovement jump) force-plate performance reports were built for Baylor Athletics athlete Skylar Zinnecker on 2026-04-14, to support a return-to-competition (RTC) decision following injury and surgery. The reports were delivered as polished, print-ready HTML files using Chart.js, and were followed by a terminology cleanup and project documentation pass.

## Key Points

- Source data was a VALD ForceDecks export (`CMJ-test-export-04_14_2026.csv`, 67 sessions spanning August 2023-April 2026), processed into HTML reports with Chart.js visualizations.
- Injury (April 12, 2025) and surgery (April 25, 2025) dates were annotated as vertical markers on the charts.
- The baseline was redefined from a full 2-year historical average to the last 4 pre-injury sessions (March 20-April 10, 2025) - a clinically more appropriate baseline for an RTC assessment - while "current" values used a 3-session rolling average from April 2, 7, and 8, 2026.
- The baseline change flipped the Lower-Limb Stiffness metric's status from "Progressing" (⚠) to "Exceeds Baseline" (✓), since the new baseline (4,693) was lower than the old one (5,477); asymmetry metrics were normalized inversely (lower % = better) for the radar chart.
- The term "nadir"/"Injury Nadir" (the post-surgery performance floor used in the recovery-percentage formula) was replaced with the clinically clearer "Post-Op Low" across all three HTML files (9 instances total), after the user found "nadir" too jargon-heavy for a clinical audience.

## Details

Styling followed Baylor's institutional branding (`#1e4d2b` green, `#b87d0a` gold) in light mode, with full print CSS (`@page` set to letter portrait, plus `-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact` to preserve colors when printed). The athlete portrait (`SZ.jpg`) was referenced via a relative path rather than embedded as base64, meaning the image and HTML files must be kept in the same directory for the reports to render correctly.

Several practical lessons emerged during the build. The `Edit` tool fails outright if its `old_string` argument doesn't match the file exactly, so the working pattern became: use `Grep` to confirm the exact existing text, re-read the surrounding context, and only then call `Edit`. A PowerShell image-dimension check required `Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Drawing` to be loaded before `[System.Drawing.Image]` could be used. Duplicate JS object keys (e.g., in a color palette) can silently survive an `Edit`, so any palette change was verified afterward with `Grep`. After all six requested deliverables were completed and saved to `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\SpecialRequests\Zinnecker_Skylar\`, a follow-up session ran `/init` to generate `CLAUDE.md` and `session_notes.md`, documenting the project for any future session that picks it back up.

# Tezino Camp Prep: SPC-Based Injury Prevention Monitoring

On 2026-06-09, a design grill session produced the full architecture for `Tezino_CampPrep` — an SPC (Statistical Process Control)-based injury prevention monitoring project for a Baylor defensive lineman (~290 lbs) who suffered consecutive mid-July injuries in 2024 and 2025 under the same mechanism and in the same calendar window. The session locked a two-tier stress model, an XmR-based monitoring frame with three embedded methodological traps to avoid, a retrospective-validation-plus-live-tool decision, and a Friday HTML dashboard design for staff review.

## Key Points

- **Injury pattern driving the project:** Tezino suffered a 5th metatarsal (MT) fracture on 2024-07-10 via an acceleration mechanism during a S&C session, then an eerily parallel hip strain in July 2025 under the same mechanism, exactly one year later. Both injuries landed in the June–July summer ramp window, establishing it as the highest-risk calendar zone. The project's core hypothesis is that the pre-injury training process was detectable before each injury, and can be monitored prospectively in 2026.
- **Two-tier stress model:** Systemic tier (tonnage, total reps, ≥80% 1RM reps, player load, distance) + foot-specific mechanical tier (acceleration count/density, HSR with a threshold appropriate for a ~290-lb DT, COD/impacts, lower-body axial lifts only). Explainability is a first-class requirement — every metric needs a plain-language "why this counts toward the foot" justification so coaching and medical staff can interpret the dashboard without an analyst present.
- **SPC frame and three methodological traps to avoid:** XmR individuals charts on a small metric panel, with control limits from a **healthy 2026 baseline window only**. Pre-injury 2024/2025 data zones are overlaid as shaded warning bands (not control limits), so "tracking with 2024" reads as an alarm rather than reassurance. Three traps: (1) setting limits from injured summers defines "in control" as the process that broke the athlete; (2) training load is intentionally non-stationary during a ramp, so chart ramp rates (delta), not raw loads; (3) too many ±3σ charts burn credibility through false alarms — the panel must be small and defensible.
- **Retrospective validation + live tool, regardless of validation outcome:** both are built. ADR-0001 mandates that the retrospective validation result be reported honestly on the dashboard itself — whether the method would have flagged the 2024 and 2025 injuries in advance, or would not have. The live monitor is a single regenerable HTML dashboard, refreshed with one command, run on Fridays, staff-presentable from day one. No automation until the manual loop proves itself over 2–3 weeks.
- **Data sources resolved:** Perch set-level data is accessible via a script reusing existing `PlayerProfiles` API credentials; the cache holds derived 1RMs from 2023-03 through 2026-04, and the raw `/v3/sets` endpoint provides set-level records — described as "just a script," not a data gap. Catapult provides player load, distance, acceleration, and HSR. PFF was demoted to context layer only (snap counts framing season load entering each offseason) — it contributes nothing to the summer ramp or XmR charts.

## Details

The project's core design challenge is the absence of a written return-to-performance progression plan for Tezino. In a standard SPC use case, control limits are derived from the prescribed training plan, and a chart flags deviation from that plan. Without an accessible plan, the substitute is process-change detection: limits derived from a healthy 2026 baseline window define "the process we know does not break him," and any departure from that process triggers investigation — independent of whether there is a formal target to deviate from. The 2024 and 2025 pre-injury data zones are retained as overlay bands rather than discarded, because they serve a forensic function: they show what "the process that led to injury" looked like, making a trajectory-toward-injury visible and alarming before threshold crossing. The critical architectural decision is that these historical injured-state bands must not be used as control limits — doing so would implicitly define "acceptable variance" to include the state the athlete was in immediately before each fracture and strain.

The two-tier model separates monitoring into systemic load (overall organismic stress per session) and foot-specific mechanical load (stressors most directly relevant to metatarsal fracture and hip strain via acceleration mechanism). This separation is both methodologically and communicatively significant. Systemic metrics give a recovery-capacity picture; foot-specific metrics isolate "the stress of the specific mechanism that broke him." Presenting them in separate tiers allows staff to distinguish "is he globally overloaded?" from "is he specifically over-stressed in the mechanism we're managing?" — different diagnostic questions requiring different interventions. The lower-body axial lift constraint for the foot-specific tier reflects the mechanical load transmission path for a 5th MT fracture: barbell compound lifts (squat, clean) load the foot axially, while upper-body or seated work does not. The ~290-lb DT classification for HSR thresholds recognizes that a high-speed running definition designed for skill positions is inappropriate for a lineman of this size — the threshold must be calibrated to the athlete's movement profile.

The grill session paused at metric panel selection, leaving a defined next-session entry point documented in `docs/grill-session-state.md`: Catapult acceleration band definitions, the appropriate HSR threshold for a 290-lb DT, which Perch lifts qualify as lower-body axial, the exact 80% 1RM cut definition, baseline window choice (what constitutes "healthy 2026 data"), and camp report dates. Project artifacts live in `Tezino_CampPrep/`: `CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/0001` (validation-honesty commitment), `docs/INJURY-TIMELINE.md`, `docs/grill-session-state.md`, and extracted data in `data/`.

- [[concepts/baylor-wtn-acwr-analysis]] — A parallel Baylor sports-science monitoring pipeline (ACWR for Women's Tennis) that also builds both a retrospective analysis and a prospective ramp model; the "build retrospective validation and live tool simultaneously, report result honestly" design principle parallels the counterfactual-plus-actual dual-model approach used there.

# Morning Email Briefing System Design

On 2026-05-21, a design spec for an automated morning email briefing system was written and committed to `Desktop/DEV/morning-briefing/docs/2026-05-21-morning-briefing-design.md`. The system ingests email and calendar sources, distills them into a structured 6-section briefing, and delivers the result from Gmail to the user's work Outlook inbox at approximately 07:30 each morning. A durable markdown copy is saved to the SecondBrain vault regardless of delivery status. The implementation plan was started but not completed — the session hit its context-window limit mid-generation. On 2026-06-08, a full manual inbox audit validated the 6-section taxonomy against real Outlook inbox content, confirming the category distribution and the practical utility of separating FYI/newsletters from actionable sections.

## Key Points

- **Delivery config:** trigger at 07:20 so the briefing arrives ~07:30; send **from** `eric.rash11@gmail.com` **to** the user's work Outlook address (primary inbox). First-arrival junk-filter risk for Exchange tenants: `eric.rash11@gmail.com` should be added to safe-senders to prevent the first delivery being routed to junk by Exchange's external-sender heuristics.
- **6-section briefing format (all approved):** NEEDS REPLY, FOLLOW UPS, MEETINGS TO SCHEDULE, FORMS/TASKS OWED, STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS (age-tagged), FYI.
- **Live validation (2026-06-08):** a full manual Outlook inbox audit produced 50 categorized items: 11 needs_reply, 3 follow_ups, 3 meetings_to_schedule, 3 forms_owed, 6 still_open, 24 FYI/newsletters. The distribution confirms the design hypothesis — FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume (48%) but require no action, while actionable obligations are concentrated in a smaller set of items. See [[concepts/inbox-triage-methodology]].
- **No auto-learning:** the allowlist and mute list are manually curated only ("30 seconds a week"); automated pattern-learning was deliberately rejected to keep behavior predictable and auditable.
- **Graceful degradation:** the system must never silently skip a briefing — if a source fails, the briefing still sends with a banner explaining what could not be retrieved. Silent failures that leave the inbox empty are worse than a degraded briefing.
- **Durable markdown copy:** each day's briefing is saved to `Desktop/SecondBrain/morning-briefings/YYYY-MM-DD.md` regardless of email delivery outcome — the vault copy is a non-negotiable design requirement, not an optional log.
- **Self-review caught a spec gap:** a checklist self-review step during implementation plan generation identified that carryover items (STILL OPEN FROM PRIOR DAYS) were not being matched against today's new email threads for resolution detection — a behavioral omission in spec Section 8 that would have caused stale items to accumulate even after they were addressed in follow-up threads. The session hit the context-window limit while patching this gap, leaving the implementation plan incomplete.

## Details

The design spec's graceful-degradation principle is the most architecturally significant decision in the system. Making the briefing always send *something* — even a degraded version with a banner such as "⚠ Calendar source unavailable today" — is a conscious choice to prefer visible, annotated failures over silent ones. A pipeline that fails silently produces no signal that something broke; a degraded briefing with an explanatory banner tells the user what the system intended and why it could not fully deliver. This framing also means the implementation must treat each source (email, calendar, carryover state) as independently degradable — no single source failure should prevent the briefing from sending.

The self-review step during implementation plan generation caught a real behavioral defect in the spec before any code was written. The `writing-plans` skill includes a review checklist pass; that pass identified that the STILL OPEN section's carryover logic (spec Section 8) lacked a mechanism for detecting when a prior-day item had since been addressed by a new email thread — a gap that would have caused the carryover list to grow monotonically rather than shrinking as items were resolved. This is a planning-layer instance of the same principle documented in [[connections/multi-stage-review-catches-agent-blind-spots]]: a second review pass with a different focus (behavioral completeness rather than format compliance) catches what the initial drafting pass misses. Two items remain outstanding before implementation can proceed: the work Outlook email address (currently a placeholder in the spec), and completion of the implementation plan (left mid-write when the session expired).

The 2026-06-08 live inbox audit (see [[concepts/inbox-triage-methodology]]) validated the 6-section taxonomy against a real Outlook inbox. The distribution — 11 needs_reply, 3 follow_ups, 3 meetings_to_schedule, 3 forms_owed, 6 still_open, 24 FYI/newsletters — confirms that FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume (48%) but require no action, while actionable items are concentrated across the 5 actionable categories. This empirical validation supports the design decision to separate FYI from actionable sections rather than interleaving them. The same structured 6-category taxonomy drives both the manual triage process and this automated daily briefing, making the taxonomy the stable architectural element across both tools — see [[connections/inbox-triage-and-morning-briefing-taxonomy]].

# Connection: Unactioned Urgent Items Age Forward Across Consecutive Digests

## The Connection

The recurring Outlook triage runs share a structural outcome that no single run makes visible: the item ranked most urgent on one day frequently reappears at the top of the next day's digest with its age counter incremented by one. The SOC "Suspicious PowerShell command line" alert topped the ranking on 2026-08-06 at 3 days outstanding and again on 2026-08-07 at 4 days (see [[concepts/outlook-inbox-triage-2026-08-07]] and [[concepts/outlook-inbox-triage-2026-08-06]]). The same shape appears in the June series, where the Catapult renewal and Playfly timecard were flagged OVERDUE across the 6-02, 6-03, 6-04, and 6-05 runs with counters incrementing daily, and in the two consecutive carryover-only days documented in [[concepts/carryover-only-email-digest]], where a digest contained no new threads at all — only the prior queue, one day older.

## Key Insight

The [[concepts/inbox-triage-methodology]] optimizes for *visibility*, not *closure*. Its age × importance heuristic guarantees that the most consequential unresolved item surfaces first every time the audit runs — which is exactly what makes the same item's repeated appearance a signal rather than noise. But because the triage is explicitly read-only (it "established a prioritized ground truth without executing replies"), correctly ranking an item has no mechanism for retiring it. The result is a system that reliably reports escalating risk while structurally unable to reduce it: a security alert can be named "highest urgency" on two consecutive mornings and still be four days unactioned.

The non-obvious implication is that a triage digest's own history is a distinct diagnostic layer. A single run tells you what is urgent; the diff between consecutive runs tells you what the triage is failing to convert into action. Items whose age counter increments across three or more digests without a category change (needs_reply never becoming resolved, forms_owed never becoming signed) identify a class of obligation that the digest format alone cannot dislodge — typically because they require an external actor (a CSM reply, a countersignature, a security team) or an action heavier than a reply. Under this reading, a repeatedly-top-ranked item should trigger an escalation different in kind from re-reading the digest, and the count of consecutive appearances — not just raw age — is the correct trigger metric. The carryover-only digests are the limit case: a day where the diff is *entirely* aging, and the digest's informational value comes almost wholly from the increment rather than from any new content.

# Inbox Triage Methodology (Structured 6-Category Audit)

A structured inbox triage is an ad-hoc deep-audit process that produces a comprehensive categorized snapshot of all pending communications in an email client. Unlike the automated morning email briefing (see [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]]), which delivers a pre-processed summary at a fixed daily time, the inbox triage is run on demand — typically when the communication queue has grown large or when a full reset of communication state is needed. On 2026-06-08, a full audit of Eric Rash's Outlook inbox at Baylor Athletics produced a structured JSON of 50 categorized items across 6 buckets, establishing a prioritized reply and follow-up plan for the session.

## Key Points

- **6-category taxonomy:** `needs_reply` (11), `follow_ups` (3), `meetings_to_schedule` (3), `forms_owed` (3), `still_open` (6), `FYI/newsletters` (24). This taxonomy mirrors the 6-section structure of [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]], making triage output directly consumable by the automated morning briefing pipeline and the [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] must-do generator.
- **Structured JSON audit:** the triage produces a machine-readable structured output categorizing all pending items before any replies are written, enabling systematic prioritization across the full queue rather than time-boxing around the first items encountered.
- **Prioritization heuristic: age × importance.** Overdue compliance items (timecards, hard-deadline forms) rank first; then aged replies sorted oldest-first; then newer but high-urgency items. The 2026-06-08 audit surfaced a 9-day-overdue Playfly LLC timecard verification as the single highest-urgency item.
- **FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume:** 24 of 50 items (48%) required no action. Segregating these into a dedicated FYI category is essential to keeping actionable items visible and preventing low-urgency volume from masking real obligations.
- **Communication debt compounds with age:** 11–13 day stale items (Quin Sandler check-in 11 days stale, Kyle Van Pelt collaboration thread 13 days stale) represent accumulated relational risk; the age-based sort within categories surfaces these items explicitly before newer but less urgent ones.

## Details

The structured inbox triage serves a different function than daily briefings or on-ramp automation. A morning briefing is a push-based system delivering a pre-processed communication summary each day; the inbox triage is a pull-based reset that generates a complete ground-truth snapshot of the full communication queue at a single point in time. The triage is most valuable when the queue has gone unmanaged for several days and the true scope of outstanding obligations is unclear. By producing a structured JSON audit before any responses are written, the triage makes the full scope visible simultaneously — enabling optimal prioritization across the entire queue rather than reactive processing of items in arrival order.

The 2026-06-08 triage revealed a characteristic distribution: FYI/newsletters (48%) were the largest single category by volume but required no action; `needs_reply` (11 items, 22%) was the most operationally important actionable category; and the three remaining actionable categories (`follow_ups`, `meetings_to_schedule`, `forms_owed`) each contained 3 items. This distribution validates the morning email briefing system's 6-section design hypothesis — that most inbox volume is low-urgency FYI, while high-urgency obligations are concentrated in a smaller set of actionable items. The Playfly LLC timecard (9 days overdue) exemplifies the `forms_owed` category's compliance-critical character: unlike email replies where a delay primarily affects relationships, an overdue timecard carries institutional consequences that escalate with each passing day. Age-based prioritization within each category makes these escalating risks visible immediately rather than requiring manual scanning for overdue items.

# Advisor Invocation Failure Modes: Unknown Domain and Missing Question

On 2026-08-14 a `/advisor fable` invocation failed on two independent grounds simultaneously, exposing the advisor skill's two distinct input-validation gates. First, no `advisors/fable.md` persona exists — the library's only persona remains `strength-and-conditioning`, with the library subtree holding `strength-and-conditioning/` and `research-papers/`. Second, the invocation supplied a domain argument but no question, so even a valid domain would have had nothing to answer. The assistant stopped rather than answering from general knowledge under an advisor's name, per the advisor skill's hard rule.

## Key Points

- **Two independent validation gates:** domain resolution (does `advisors/<domain>.md` exist?) and question presence (was an actual question supplied?). A malformed invocation can fail both at once, and each failure mode has a different remedy.
- **Refusal on unknown domain is the correct behavior, not a bug:** answering a "fable" question from parametric model knowledge while wearing an advisor label would produce output indistinguishable from a grounded advisor response — the exact failure mode the advisor system's hard rule exists to prevent.
- **Three-way remediation menu:** the user's options were (a) invoke the `/fable-mode` skill they likely meant, (b) ask the existing `strength-and-conditioning` advisor an actual question, or (c) stand up a new `fable` persona — requiring `advisors/fable.md` plus grounding material ingested via `/ingest-book`, per `CREATING-ADVISORS.md` at the library root.
- **Library coverage remains thin:** a single persona, unchanged since the 2026-06-12 pilot and the 2026-07-09 no-argument listing invocation. Two of the three documented `/advisor` invocations to date have been non-question invocations that exercised routing rather than retrieval.
- **No-argument vs. bad-argument produce different behaviors:** invoking `/advisor` with no domain (2026-07-09) yields a listing of available personas; invoking with an unrecognized domain (2026-08-14) yields a refusal plus a remediation menu. Both are discovery/routing paths, not grounded answers.

## Details

The advisor skill's architecture makes the refusal path structurally necessary. Because an advisor's value proposition is that its responses trace to specific ingested entries, any response emitted under an advisor label without a resolvable persona and a grounded corpus behind it silently breaks the system's core contract. The 2026-06-12 pilot established this discipline for the *off-library question* case — a valid persona asked a question outside its ingested corpus must disclose the grounding gap and refuse, even when memsearch returns 0.98 similarity scores. The 2026-08-14 session extends the same discipline one level earlier in the pipeline: an *unresolvable persona* must also refuse, because there is no corpus at all to check a question against. The two refusals are the same rule applied at different stages — corpus-level grounding failure versus persona-level resolution failure.

The missing-question observation is a smaller but practically useful finding. The advisor skill accepts a domain argument, and a domain-only invocation is syntactically well-formed; nothing in the argument shape signals that the invocation is incomplete. This means a user can supply a correct domain and still receive no grounded answer, which would be confusing if the skill silently produced a generic domain summary instead of asking for the question. Explicitly flagging "you gave me a domain but no question" is a cheap disambiguation that prevents the skill from guessing at intent. It also implies a design consideration: a domain-only invocation could reasonably resolve to a *scope summary* for that persona (what it is grounded in, what it can answer) rather than an error, which would parallel the no-argument listing behavior already observed on 2026-07-09.

The remediation menu is worth noting as a pattern in its own right. Rather than picking one interpretation of the ambiguous input, the assistant enumerated the three plausible intents and their respective costs — the skill invocation is free, the existing-advisor path needs only a question, and the new-persona path requires both authoring work and an ingestion run. This puts the disambiguation decision with the user while making the relative effort of each branch explicit, which matters here because option (c) is materially more expensive than (a) or (b).

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

# Tezino Camp Prep: SPC-Based Injury Prevention Monitoring

On 2026-06-09, a design grill session produced the full architecture for `Tezino_CampPrep` — an SPC (Statistical Process Control)-based injury prevention monitoring project for a Baylor defensive lineman (~290 lbs) who suffered consecutive mid-July injuries in 2024 and 2025 under the same mechanism and in the same calendar window. The session locked a two-tier stress model, an XmR-based monitoring frame with three embedded methodological traps to avoid, a retrospective-validation-plus-live-tool decision, and a Friday HTML dashboard design for staff review.

## Key Points

- **Injury pattern driving the project:** Tezino suffered a 5th metatarsal (MT) fracture on 2024-07-10 via an acceleration mechanism during a S&C session, then an eerily parallel hip strain in July 2025 under the same mechanism, exactly one year later. Both injuries landed in the June–July summer ramp window, establishing it as the highest-risk calendar zone. The project's core hypothesis is that the pre-injury training process was detectable before each injury, and can be monitored prospectively in 2026.
- **Two-tier stress model:** Systemic tier (tonnage, total reps, ≥80% 1RM reps, player load, distance) + foot-specific mechanical tier (acceleration count/density, HSR with a threshold appropriate for a ~290-lb DT, COD/impacts, lower-body axial lifts only). Explainability is a first-class requirement — every metric needs a plain-language "why this counts toward the foot" justification so coaching and medical staff can interpret the dashboard without an analyst present.
- **SPC frame and three methodological traps to avoid:** XmR individuals charts on a small metric panel, with control limits from a **healthy 2026 baseline window only**. Pre-injury 2024/2025 data zones are overlaid as shaded warning bands (not control limits), so "tracking with 2024" reads as an alarm rather than reassurance. Three traps: (1) setting limits from injured summers defines "in control" as the process that broke the athlete; (2) training load is intentionally non-stationary during a ramp, so chart ramp rates (delta), not raw loads; (3) too many ±3σ charts burn credibility through false alarms — the panel must be small and defensible.
- **Retrospective validation + live tool, regardless of validation outcome:** both are built. ADR-0001 mandates that the retrospective validation result be reported honestly on the dashboard itself — whether the method would have flagged the 2024 and 2025 injuries in advance, or would not have. The live monitor is a single regenerable HTML dashboard, refreshed with one command, run on Fridays, staff-presentable from day one. No automation until the manual loop proves itself over 2–3 weeks.
- **Data sources resolved:** Perch set-level data is accessible via a script reusing existing `PlayerProfiles` API credentials; the cache holds derived 1RMs from 2023-03 through 2026-04, and the raw `/v3/sets` endpoint provides set-level records — described as "just a script," not a data gap. Catapult provides player load, distance, acceleration, and HSR. PFF was demoted to context layer only (snap counts framing season load entering each offseason) — it contributes nothing to the summer ramp or XmR charts.

## Details

The project's core design challenge is the absence of a written return-to-performance progression plan for Tezino. In a standard SPC use case, control limits are derived from the prescribed training plan, and a chart flags deviation from that plan. Without an accessible plan, the substitute is process-change detection: limits derived from a healthy 2026 baseline window define "the process we know does not break him," and any departure from that process triggers investigation — independent of whether there is a formal target to deviate from. The 2024 and 2025 pre-injury data zones are retained as overlay bands rather than discarded, because they serve a forensic function: they show what "the process that led to injury" looked like, making a trajectory-toward-injury visible and alarming before threshold crossing. The critical architectural decision is that these historical injured-state bands must not be used as control limits — doing so would implicitly define "acceptable variance" to include the state the athlete was in immediately before each fracture and strain.

The two-tier model separates monitoring into systemic load (overall organismic stress per session) and foot-specific mechanical load (stressors most directly relevant to metatarsal fracture and hip strain via acceleration mechanism). This separation is both methodologically and communicatively significant. Systemic metrics give a recovery-capacity picture; foot-specific metrics isolate "the stress of the specific mechanism that broke him." Presenting them in separate tiers allows staff to distinguish "is he globally overloaded?" from "is he specifically over-stressed in the mechanism we're managing?" — different diagnostic questions requiring different interventions. The lower-body axial lift constraint for the foot-specific tier reflects the mechanical load transmission path for a 5th MT fracture: barbell compound lifts (squat, clean) load the foot axially, while upper-body or seated work does not. The ~290-lb DT classification for HSR thresholds recognizes that a high-speed running definition designed for skill positions is inappropriate for a lineman of this size — the threshold must be calibrated to the athlete's movement profile.

The grill session paused at metric panel selection, leaving a defined next-session entry point documented in `docs/grill-session-state.md`: Catapult acceleration band definitions, the appropriate HSR threshold for a 290-lb DT, which Perch lifts qualify as lower-body axial, the exact 80% 1RM cut definition, baseline window choice (what constitutes "healthy 2026 data"), and camp report dates. Project artifacts live in `Tezino_CampPrep/`: `CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/0001` (validation-honesty commitment), `docs/INJURY-TIMELINE.md`, `docs/grill-session-state.md`, and extracted data in `data/`.

The system ingests email and calendar sources, distills them into a structured 6-section briefing, and delivers the result from Gmail to the user's work Outlook inbox at approximately 07:30 each morning. # Connection: Unactioned Urgent Items Age Forward Across Consecutive Digests

## The Connection

The recurring Outlook triage runs share a structural outcome that no single run makes visible: the item ranked most urgent on one day frequently reappears at the top of the next day's digest with its age counter incremented by one. The SOC "Suspicious PowerShell command line" alert topped the ranking on 2026-08-06 at 3 days outstanding and again on 2026-08-07 at 4 days (see [[concepts/outlook-inbox-triage-2026-08-07]] and [[concepts/outlook-inbox-triage-2026-08-06]]). The same shape appears in the June series, where the Catapult renewal and Playfly timecard were flagged OVERDUE across the 6-02, 6-03, 6-04, and 6-05 runs with counters incrementing daily, and in the two consecutive carryover-only days documented in [[concepts/carryover-only-email-digest]], where a digest contained no new threads at all — only the prior queue, one day older.

## Key Insight

The [[concepts/inbox-triage-methodology]] optimizes for *visibility*, not *closure*. Its age × importance heuristic guarantees that the most consequential unresolved item surfaces first every time the audit runs — which is exactly what makes the same item's repeated appearance a signal rather than noise. But because the triage is explicitly read-only (it "established a prioritized ground truth without executing replies"), correctly ranking an item has no mechanism for retiring it. The result is a system that reliably reports escalating risk while structurally unable to reduce it: a security alert can be named "highest urgency" on two consecutive mornings and still be four days unactioned.

The non-obvious implication is that a triage digest's own history is a distinct diagnostic layer. A single run tells you what is urgent; the diff between consecutive runs tells you what the triage is failing to convert into action. Items whose age counter increments across three or more digests without a category change (needs_reply never becoming resolved, forms_owed never becoming signed) identify a class of obligation that the digest format alone cannot dislodge — typically because they require an external actor (a CSM reply, a countersignature, a security team) or an action heavier than a reply. Under this reading, a repeatedly-top-ranked item should trigger an escalation different in kind from re-reading the digest, and the count of consecutive appearances — not just raw age — is the correct trigger metric. The carryover-only digests are the limit case: a day where the diff is *entirely* aging, and the digest's informational value comes almost wholly from the increment rather than from any new content.

- 2026-08-07 (11:06): the same SOC alert, now 4 days outstanding, again ranked highest-urgency and again left as an action item ("Investigate/respond to SOC alert (4 days outstanding — security incident)").

# Inbox Triage Methodology (Structured 6-Category Audit)

A structured inbox triage is an ad-hoc deep-audit process that produces a comprehensive categorized snapshot of all pending communications in an email client. Unlike the automated morning email briefing (see [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]]), which delivers a pre-processed summary at a fixed daily time, the inbox triage is run on demand — typically when the communication queue has grown large or when a full reset of communication state is needed. On 2026-06-08, a full audit of Eric Rash's Outlook inbox at Baylor Athletics produced a structured JSON of 50 categorized items across 6 buckets, establishing a prioritized reply and follow-up plan for the session.

## Key Points

- **6-category taxonomy:** `needs_reply` (11), `follow_ups` (3), `meetings_to_schedule` (3), `forms_owed` (3), `still_open` (6), `FYI/newsletters` (24). This taxonomy mirrors the 6-section structure of [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]], making triage output directly consumable by the automated morning briefing pipeline and the [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] must-do generator.
- **Structured JSON audit:** the triage produces a machine-readable structured output categorizing all pending items before any replies are written, enabling systematic prioritization across the full queue rather than time-boxing around the first items encountered.
- **Prioritization heuristic: age × importance.** Overdue compliance items (timecards, hard-deadline forms) rank first; then aged replies sorted oldest-first; then newer but high-urgency items. The 2026-06-08 audit surfaced a 9-day-overdue Playfly LLC timecard verification as the single highest-urgency item.
- **FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume:** 24 of 50 items (48%) required no action. Segregating these into a dedicated FYI category is essential to keeping actionable items visible and preventing low-urgency volume from masking real obligations.
- **Communication debt compounds with age:** 11–13 day stale items (Quin Sandler check-in 11 days stale, Kyle Van Pelt collaboration thread 13 days stale) represent accumulated relational risk; the age-based sort within categories surfaces these items explicitly before newer but less urgent ones.

## Details

The structured inbox triage serves a different function than daily briefings or on-ramp automation. A morning briefing is a push-based system delivering a pre-processed communication summary each day; the inbox triage is a pull-based reset that generates a complete ground-truth snapshot of the full communication queue at a single point in time. The triage is most valuable when the queue has gone unmanaged for several days and the true scope of outstanding obligations is unclear. By producing a structured JSON audit before any responses are written, the triage makes the full scope visible simultaneously — enabling optimal prioritization across the entire queue rather than reactive processing of items in arrival order.

# Advisor Invocation Failure Modes: Unknown Domain and Missing Question

On 2026-08-14 a `/advisor fable` invocation failed on two independent grounds simultaneously, exposing the advisor skill's two distinct input-validation gates. First, no `advisors/fable.md` persona exists — the library's only persona remains `strength-and-conditioning`, with the library subtree holding `strength-and-conditioning/` and `research-papers/`. Second, the invocation supplied a domain argument but no question, so even a valid domain would have had nothing to answer. The assistant stopped rather than answering from general knowledge under an advisor's name, per the advisor skill's hard rule.

## Key Points

- **Two independent validation gates:** domain resolution (does `advisors/<domain>.md` exist?) and question presence (was an actual question supplied?). A malformed invocation can fail both at once, and each failure mode has a different remedy.
- **Refusal on unknown domain is the correct behavior, not a bug:** answering a "fable" question from parametric model knowledge while wearing an advisor label would produce output indistinguishable from a grounded advisor response — the exact failure mode the advisor system's hard rule exists to prevent.
- **Three-way remediation menu:** the user's options were (a) invoke the `/fable-mode` skill they likely meant, (b) ask the existing `strength-and-conditioning` advisor an actual question, or (c) stand up a new `fable` persona — requiring `advisors/fable.md` plus grounding material ingested via `/ingest-book`, per `CREATING-ADVISORS.md` at the library root.
- **Library coverage remains thin:** a single persona, unchanged since the 2026-06-12 pilot and the 2026-07-09 no-argument listing invocation. Two of the three documented `/advisor` invocations to date have been non-question invocations that exercised routing rather than retrieval.
- **No-argument vs. bad-argument produce different behaviors:** invoking `/advisor` with no domain (2026-07-09) yields a listing of available personas; invoking with an unrecognized domain (2026-08-14) yields a refusal plus a remediation menu. Both are discovery/routing paths, not grounded answers.

## Details

The advisor skill's architecture makes the refusal path structurally necessary. Because an advisor's value proposition is that its responses trace to specific ingested entries, any response emitted under an advisor label without a resolvable persona and a grounded corpus behind it silently breaks the system's core contract. The 2026-06-12 pilot established this discipline for the *off-library question* case — a valid persona asked a question outside its ingested corpus must disclose the grounding gap and refuse, even when memsearch returns 0.98 similarity scores. The 2026-08-14 session extends the same discipline one level earlier in the pipeline: an *unresolvable persona* must also refuse, because there is no corpus at all to check a question against. The two refusals are the same rule applied at different stages — corpus-level grounding failure versus persona-level resolution failure.

The missing-question observation is a smaller but practically useful finding. The advisor skill accepts a domain argument, and a domain-only invocation is syntactically well-formed; nothing in the argument shape signals that the invocation is incomplete. This means a user can supply a correct domain and still receive no grounded answer, which would be confusing if the skill silently produced a generic domain summary instead of asking for the question. Explicitly flagging "you gave me a domain but no question" is a cheap disambiguation that prevents the skill from guessing at intent. It also implies a design consideration: a domain-only invocation could reasonably resolve to a *scope summary* for that persona (what it is grounded in, what it can answer) rather than an error, which would parallel the no-argument listing behavior already observed on 2026-07-09.

The remediation menu is worth noting as a pattern in its own right. Rather than picking one interpretation of the ambiguous input, the assistant enumerated the three plausible intents and their respective costs — the skill invocation is free, the existing-advisor path needs only a question, and the new-persona path requires both authoring work and an ingestion run. This puts the disambiguation decision with the user while making the relative effort of each branch explicit, which matters here because option (c) is materially more expensive than (a) or (b).

# Connection: The Reference Window Decides the Verdict

## The Connection

Two Baylor Athletics monitoring builds, eight weeks apart and answering opposite questions — is this athlete recovered? is this athlete heading toward injury? — arrived at the same methodological hinge: which slice of history is allowed to define "normal." In [[concepts/skylar-zinnecker-cmj-rtc-reports]], the CMJ baseline was moved from a two-year historical average to the last four pre-injury sessions (March 20–April 10, 2025), and that single change flipped Lower-Limb Stiffness from "Progressing (⚠)" to "Exceeds Baseline (✓)" — the new reference (4,693) sat below the old one (5,477). In [[concepts/tezino-camp-prep-spc-monitoring]], the corresponding decision was made pre-emptively and written into the architecture: XmR control limits derive from a **healthy 2026 baseline window only**, with the 2024 and 2025 pre-injury zones retained as shaded overlay bands rather than limits, because "setting limits from injured summers defines 'in control' as the process that broke the athlete."

## Key Insight

Neither project's headline metric changed; only the denominator did — and in both cases the denominator carried the entire clinical claim. This makes the reference window, not the metric panel, the highest-leverage design decision in athlete monitoring, and the one most likely to be made implicitly by whatever data happens to be in the export.

The two projects also show the failure mode is directional, not random. Zinnecker's original two-year average silently *inflated* the bar by folding in a healthier, further-past athlete, making a recovered athlete look still-impaired. Tezino's hypothetical limits-from-injured-summers would have *deflated* the bar, making a trajectory toward fracture look statistically unremarkable. Same error class — contaminated reference window — opposite consequences: one produces false alarms and stalls a return-to-competition, the other produces false reassurance and misses the thing the system exists to catch. Which direction you get depends entirely on whether the contaminating period was better or worse than the state you actually want to compare against.

The transferable move is what Tezino did with the discarded data. Zinnecker's old two-year baseline was simply replaced; Tezino kept the contaminated window but demoted it from *reference* to *overlay* — the injured summers still appear on the chart, doing forensic work ("this is what the process that broke him looked like"), while no longer defining acceptable variance. That demotion, rather than deletion, is the generalizable pattern: a contaminated window is usually still the most informative comparison available, provided it is drawn as a warning band and never as a limit. A useful default for any future report: state the reference window explicitly on the artifact itself, and state what was *excluded* from it and why — because a reader who sees only "Exceeds Baseline ✓" has no way to recover the decision that produced it.

## Key Points

- **A baseline change, not a data change, flipped a clinical status.** Zinnecker's Lower-Limb Stiffness moved from ⚠ to ✓ purely because the reference window narrowed from two years to four pre-injury sessions.
- **Tezino encodes the same rule as an architectural constraint.** Control limits come from a healthy 2026 window only; the 2024/2025 pre-injury zones are overlay bands, explicitly barred from becoming limits.
- **The error is directional.** A too-broad healthy window inflates the bar (false alarm, stalled RTC); an injured-state window deflates it (false reassurance, missed injury).
- **Contaminated windows are demoted, not deleted.** Tezino's forensic overlay bands make "tracking with 2024" read as an alarm — retaining the data's diagnostic value while stripping its normative authority.
- **The reference window should be a stated artifact.** Both reports are consumed by clinical and coaching staff who see only the verdict; the window and its exclusions belong on the deliverable, alongside the metric.

## Details

The Zinnecker case is instructive precisely because the correction was made mid-build rather than at design time. The initial reports were generated against the full 67-session export spanning August 2023–April 2026 — the natural default, since that is what the VALD ForceDecks CSV contained. Only on inspection did the mismatch surface: an RTC assessment asks "has this athlete returned to the person they were immediately before the injury," and a two-year average answers a different question ("has this athlete returned to their multi-season typical"), one that includes developmental periods, other training blocks, and possibly a different physical maturity. The four-session pre-injury window is a narrower, noisier estimate — four data points is thin — but it is an estimate of the right quantity. The trade the project made, implicitly, was statistical precision for construct validity, and the stiffness metric flipping status is the visible price and payoff of that trade.

Tezino inverts the sequence: the reference-window question was resolved in the design grill session, before a chart existed, and elevated to one of three named methodological traps. That framing is what generalizes. The other two traps in that list — non-stationarity during a deliberate ramp (chart deltas, not raw loads) and credibility burn from too many ±3σ charts — are both, at bottom, about the same thing: an SPC chart's alarms only mean something if the "in control" region encodes a defensible claim about what normal should be. A ramp is *supposed* to trend, so a chart limit built on raw load flags the intended program; limits built on injured summers bless the pre-fracture process; a wide panel of charts means some limit somewhere is always being crossed. Each trap is a way the reference standard stops corresponding to the thing staff care about, while the chart continues to look authoritative.

The absence in Tezino makes the point sharpest. There is no written return-to-performance progression plan for the athlete, so there is no prescribed target to chart deviation from — the ordinary SPC setup is unavailable. The substitute is process-change detection against a healthy-window baseline: "the process we know does not break him." That is a reference window standing in for a plan. Which means the window is not a statistical nicety layered on top of the monitoring system — in this project it *is* the monitoring system's definition of correct, the only thing distinguishing a meaningful alarm from a chart artifact. # Connection: Refuse Upstream or Verify Downstream — Two Defenses Against Plausible Output

## The Connection

Both sessions confront output that is indistinguishable, at the surface, from correct output. In [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]], a repair agent returned citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 with hallucinated author lists that correctly identified the papers' topics — plausible enough to commit — and a photo that "failed" only because the preview server did not serve images. In [[concepts/advisor-invocation-failure-modes]], the failure mode being defended against is exactly the same shape: an answer to a "fable" question emitted under an advisor label "would produce output indistinguishable from a grounded advisor response."

But the two respond in opposite directions along the pipeline. The advisor skill halts *before* generating: no `advisors/fable.md`, no corpus, therefore no answer, plus a three-way remediation menu. The 2026-04-22 sessions let the output exist and then changed the *verification channel* — PyPDF2 to read the actual PDF text, Chrome via `file://` to render the actual HTML — stepping down to a more primitive layer closer to ground truth.

## Key Insight

The choice between the two is not stylistic; it is determined by whether a *checkable precondition* exists upstream of generation. The advisor case has one that is cheap and binary: does the persona file resolve on disk? A filesystem check costs nothing and settles the question completely, so refusing is strictly better than generating and auditing. The citation case has no such gate — nothing about "fix the author list for ID 286" is malformed, the agent has genuine access to the papers, and the request is well-posed. There is no precondition to fail on, so the only available defense is downstream, and it must be a channel the generating layer did not mediate.

This yields a practical rule for where to spend defensive effort: look first for a precondition that can be checked without doing the work, because that check is nearly free and its failure is unambiguous. Only when no such precondition exists — when the request is well-formed and the failure is in the *content* of a competent-looking result — does the more expensive downstream discipline become necessary. Spending verification effort on cases that a precondition check would have caught is waste; assuming a precondition check covers cases where none exists is the more dangerous error, because it produces confidence without coverage.

The two also differ in what they can guarantee. A precondition refusal is complete for the class it covers — an unresolvable persona *cannot* slip through. Downstream verification is only as good as the independence of the check: opening the HTML in Chrome worked because Chrome does not share the preview server's image-serving limitation, and PyPDF2 worked because it does not share the agent's summarization step. A "verification" that reuses the same intermediate layer verifies nothing while feeling like diligence — which is why the advisor system's other documented refusal, on a 0.98 memsearch similarity score, matters: a high retrieval score is the generating layer's own confidence, not an independent channel.

## Key Points

- **Same underlying hazard:** output whose surface form carries no signal of its own invalidity — a plausible author list, a confident advisor answer.
- **Opposite pipeline positions:** the advisor halts before generation on an unmet precondition; the citation/photo cases accept generation and re-check through an independent channel.
- **The selector is precondition availability.** A cheap binary gate (does the persona file exist?) makes refusal strictly superior; a well-formed request with no gate leaves only downstream verification.
- **Guarantees differ in kind.** Precondition refusal is complete for its class; downstream verification is only as strong as the check's independence from the layer that produced the output.
- **Reusing the generating layer's own confidence is not verification.** A 0.98 similarity score, like a preview server's render, is mediated by the thing under test.

## Details

The advisor architecture is unusually explicit about why refusal is load-bearing rather than merely conservative. An advisor's entire value proposition is that its responses trace to specific ingested entries; an ungrounded response wearing the label does not degrade the system's output quality so much as void its contract, silently. That silence is the operative property — a user cannot tell from the response text whether the corpus was consulted. This is precisely why the two documented refusals sit at different stages of the same pipeline: the 2026-06-12 pilot refused an in-scope persona asked an off-corpus question, and the 2026-08-14 session refused an unresolvable persona before any question was even considered. The 2026-08-14 case is the cheaper of the two to enforce, because it requires no judgment about corpus coverage — just a file lookup.

The 2026-04-22 sessions occupy the region where that cheapness is unavailable. Nothing in the batch-import task presents a gate: the repair agent was given a legitimate job, had access to the source material, and produced output correct in the dimension easiest to check (topic identification) and wrong in the dimension requiring the source (author lists). Notably, the topic-level correctness is what made the citations dangerous — a wholly wrong output would have been caught immediately, whereas partial competence is what buys a hallucination its credibility. The fix was not to re-run the agent with better instructions but to change what counted as confirmation, which is the structurally correct response when the failure lives inside plausible-looking content rather than at an input boundary.

The photo case is the useful counterweight, because there the downstream verification *exonerated* the work. The HTML and the relative path were both correct; the preview server simply did not serve image files. Had the response been "the agent was wrong, regenerate," the outcome would have been wasted effort chasing a non-defect. This is the symmetric risk of downstream-only defense: without an independent channel you cannot distinguish a broken artifact from a broken observer, and the default assumption tends to blame the artifact. It also explains why the advisor's remediation menu is more than politeness — enumerating the three plausible intents (invoke `/fable-mode`, ask the existing persona, author a new one) and their relative costs converts a bare refusal into a routing decision the user can actually make, which is the upstream analogue of choosing the right verification channel downstream.
